# **Appendix M. Glossary**

This is a list of terms and their meaning in the context of PostgreSQL and relational database systems in general.

ACID *[Atomicity](#page-184-0)*, *[Consistency](#page-186-0)*, *[Isolation](#page-189-0)*, and *[Durability](#page-188-0)*. This set of

properties of database transactions is intended to guarantee validity in concurrent operation and even in event of errors, power fail-

ures, etc.

<span id="page-184-6"></span>Aggregate function (routine) A *[function](#page-188-1)* that combines (*aggregates*) multiple input values, for

example by counting, averaging or adding, yielding a single out-

put value.

For more information, see Section 9.21.

See Also [Window function \(routine\)](#page-197-0).

Analytic function See [Window function \(routine\).](#page-197-0)

<span id="page-184-1"></span>Analyze (operation) The act of collecting statistics from data in *[tables](#page-194-0)* and other *[rela-](#page-191-0)*

*[tions](#page-191-0)* to help the *[query planner](#page-191-1)* to make decisions about how to

execute *[queries](#page-191-2)*.

(Don't confuse this term with the ANALYZE option to the EX-

PLAIN command.)

For more information, see ANALYZE.

<span id="page-184-7"></span>Atomic In reference to a *[datum](#page-187-1)*: the fact that its value cannot be broken

down into smaller components.

In reference to a *[database transaction](#page-194-1)*: see *[atomicity](#page-184-0)*.

<span id="page-184-0"></span>Atomicity The property of a *[transaction](#page-194-1)* that either all its operations com-

plete as a single unit or none do. In addition, if a system failure occurs during the execution of a transaction, no partial results are

visible after recovery. This is one of the ACID properties.

<span id="page-184-4"></span>Attribute An element with a certain name and data type found within a *[tuple](#page-195-0)*.

<span id="page-184-3"></span>Autovacuum (process) A set of background processes that routinely perform *[vacuum](#page-196-0)*

and *[analyze](#page-184-1)* operations. The *[auxiliary process](#page-184-2)* that coordinates the work and is always present (unless autovacuum is disabled) is known as the *autovacuum launcher*, and the processes that carry

out the tasks are known as the *autovacuum workers*.

For more information, see Section 25.1.6.

<span id="page-184-2"></span>Auxiliary process A process within an *[instance](#page-189-1)* that is in charge of some specific

background task for the instance. The auxiliary processes consist of the *[autovacuum launcher](#page-184-3)* (but not the autovacuum workers), the *[background writer](#page-185-0)*, the *[checkpointer](#page-186-1)*, the *[logger](#page-190-1)*, the *[startup](#page-194-2) [process](#page-194-2)*, the *[WAL archiver](#page-196-1)*, the *[WAL receiver](#page-197-1)* (but not the *[WAL](#page-197-2)*

*[senders](#page-197-2)*), and the *[WAL writer](#page-197-3)*.

<span id="page-184-5"></span>Backend (process) Process of an *[instance](#page-189-1)* which acts on behalf of a *[client session](#page-193-0)* and

handles its requests.

(Don't confuse this term with the similar terms *[Background Work](#page-185-1)[er](#page-185-1)* or *[Background Writer](#page-185-0)*).

<span id="page-185-1"></span>

Background worker (process) Process within an *[instance](#page-189-1)*, which runs system- or user-supplied code. Serves as infrastructure for several features in PostgreSQL, such as *[logical replication](#page-192-0)* and *[parallel queries](#page-190-2)*. In addition, *[Ex](#page-188-2)[tensions](#page-188-2)* can add custom background worker processes.

For more information, see Chapter 48.

<span id="page-185-0"></span>

Background writer (process) An *[auxiliary process](#page-184-2)* that writes dirty *[data pages](#page-187-2)* from *[shared](#page-193-1) [memory](#page-193-1)* to the file system. It wakes up periodically, but works only for a short period in order to distribute its expensive I/O activity over time to avoid generating larger I/O peaks which could block other processes.

For more information, see Section 20.4.5.

Base Backup A binary copy of all *[database cluster](#page-187-3)* files. It is generated by the tool pg\_basebackup. In combination with WAL files it can be used as the starting point for recovery, log shipping, or streaming replication.

Bloat Space in data pages which does not contain current row versions, such as unused (free) space or outdated row versions.

<span id="page-185-2"></span>

Bootstrap superuser The first *[user](#page-195-1)* initialized in a *[database cluster](#page-187-3)*.

This user owns all system catalog tables in each database. It is also the role from which all granted permissions originate. Because of these things, this role may not be dropped.

This role also behaves as a normal *[database superuser](#page-187-4)*.

Buffer Access Strategy Some operations will access a large number of *[pages](#page-187-2)*. A *Buffer Access Strategy* helps to prevent these operations from evicting too many pages from *[shared buffers](#page-193-1)*.

> A Buffer Access Strategy sets up references to a limited number of *[shared buffers](#page-193-1)* and reuses them circularly. When the operation requires a new page, a victim buffer is chosen from the buffers in the strategy ring, which may require flushing the page's dirty data and possibly also unflushed *[WAL](#page-197-4)* to permanent storage.

> Buffer Access Strategies are used for various operations such as sequential scans of large tables, VACUUM, COPY, CREATE TA-BLE AS SELECT, ALTER TABLE, CREATE DATABASE, CREATE INDEX, and CLUSTER.

<span id="page-185-3"></span>Cast A conversion of a *[datum](#page-187-1)* from its current data type to another data

type.

For more information, see CREATE CAST.

Catalog The SQL standard uses this term to indicate what is called a *[data-](#page-187-5)*

*[base](#page-187-5)* in PostgreSQL's terminology.

(Don't confuse this term with *[system catalog](#page-194-3)*).

For more information, see Section 23.1.

Check constraint A type of *[constraint](#page-186-2)* defined on a *[relation](#page-191-0)* which restricts the values allowed in one or more *[attributes](#page-184-4)*. The check constraint can make reference to any attribute of the same row in the relation, but cannot reference other rows of the same relation or other relations.

For more information, see Section 5.4.

<span id="page-186-3"></span>Checkpoint A point in the *[WAL](#page-197-4)* sequence at which it is guaranteed that the heap and index data files have been updated with all information from *[shared memory](#page-193-1)* modified before that checkpoint; a *checkpoint record* is written and flushed to WAL to mark that point.

> A checkpoint is also the act of carrying out all the actions that are necessary to reach a checkpoint as defined above. This process is initiated when predefined conditions are met, such as a specified amount of time has passed, or a certain volume of records has been written; or it can be invoked by the user with the command CHECKPOINT.

For more information, see Section 30.5.

<span id="page-186-1"></span>

Checkpointer (process) An *[auxiliary process](#page-184-2)* that is responsible for executing *[check-](#page-186-3)*

*[points](#page-186-3)*.

Class (archaic) See [Relation.](#page-191-0)

<span id="page-186-8"></span>

Client (process) Any process, possibly remote, that establishes a *[session](#page-193-0)* by *[con](#page-186-4)[necting](#page-186-4)* to an *[instance](#page-189-1)* to interact with a *[database](#page-187-5)*.

<span id="page-186-5"></span>

Cluster owner The operating system user that owns the *[data directory](#page-187-6)* and under which the postgres process is run. It is required that this user exist prior to creating a new *[database cluster](#page-187-3)*.

> On operating systems with a root user, said user is not allowed to be the cluster owner.

<span id="page-186-7"></span>

Column An *[attribute](#page-184-4)* found in a *[table](#page-194-0)* or *[view](#page-196-2)*.

<span id="page-186-6"></span>

Commit The act of finalizing a *[transaction](#page-194-1)* within the *[database](#page-187-5)*, which makes it visible to other transactions and assures its *[durability](#page-188-0)*.

For more information, see COMMIT.

<span id="page-186-9"></span>

Concurrency The concept that multiple independent operations happen within the *[database](#page-187-5)* at the same time. In PostgreSQL, concurrency is controlled by the *[multiversion concurrency control](#page-190-3)* mechanism.

<span id="page-186-4"></span>

Connection An established line of communication between a client process and a *[backend](#page-184-5)* process, usually over a network, supporting a *[ses](#page-193-0)[sion](#page-193-0)*. This term is sometimes used as a synonym for session.

For more information, see Section 20.3.

<span id="page-186-0"></span>

Consistency The property that the data in the *[database](#page-187-5)* is always in compliance with *[integrity constraints](#page-186-2)*. Transactions may be allowed to violate some of the constraints transiently before it commits, but if such violations are not resolved by the time it commits, such a transaction is automatically *[rolled back](#page-192-1)*. This is one of the ACID properties.

<span id="page-186-2"></span>

Constraint A restriction on the values of data allowed within a *[table](#page-194-0)*, or in attributes of a *[domain](#page-187-0)*.

2949

For more information, see Section 5.4.

Cumulative Statistics System A system which, if enabled, accumulates statistical information

about the *[instance](#page-189-1)*'s activities.

For more information, see Section 28.2.

Data area See [Data directory](#page-187-6).

<span id="page-187-5"></span>Database A named collection of *[local SQL objects](#page-193-2)*.

For more information, see Section 23.1.

<span id="page-187-3"></span>Database cluster A collection of databases and global SQL objects, and their com-

mon static and dynamic metadata. Sometimes referred to as a *cluster*. A database cluster is created using the initdb program.

In PostgreSQL, the term *cluster* is also sometimes used to refer to an instance. (Don't confuse this term with the SQL command

CLUSTER.)

See also *[cluster owner](#page-186-5)*, the operating-system owner of a cluster, and *[bootstrap superuser](#page-185-2)*, the PostgreSQL owner of a cluster.

Database server See [Instance](#page-189-1).

<span id="page-187-4"></span>Database superuser A role having *superuser status* (see Section 22.2).

Frequently referred to as *superuser*.

<span id="page-187-6"></span>Data directory The base directory on the file system of a *[server](#page-193-3)* that contains all

data files and subdirectories associated with a *[database cluster](#page-187-3)* (with the exception of *[tablespaces](#page-194-4)*, and optionally *[WAL](#page-197-4)*). The environment variable PGDATA is commonly used to refer to the data

directory.

A *[cluster](#page-187-3)*'s storage space comprises the data directory plus any

additional tablespaces.

For more information, see Section 73.1.

<span id="page-187-2"></span>Data page The basic structure used to store relation data. All pages are of

the same size. Data pages are typically stored on disk, each in a specific file, and can be read to *[shared buffers](#page-193-1)* where they can be modified, becoming *dirty*. They become clean when written to disk. New pages, which initially exist in memory only, are also

dirty until written.

<span id="page-187-1"></span>Datum The internal representation of one value of an SQL data type.

Delete An SQL command which removes *[rows](#page-195-0)* from a given *[table](#page-194-0)* or

*[relation](#page-191-0)*.

For more information, see DELETE.

<span id="page-187-0"></span>Domain A user-defined data type that is based on another underlying data

type. It acts the same as the underlying type except for possibly

restricting the set of allowed values.

For more information, see Section 8.18.

<span id="page-188-0"></span>Durability The assurance that once a *[transaction](#page-194-1)* has been *[committed](#page-186-6)*, the

changes remain even after a system failure or crash. This is one

of the ACID properties.

Epoch See [Transaction ID](#page-195-2).

<span id="page-188-2"></span>Extension A software add-on package that can be installed on an *[instance](#page-189-1)*

to get extra features.

For more information, see Section 38.17.

<span id="page-188-7"></span>File segment A physical file which stores data for a given *[relation](#page-191-0)*. File seg-

ments are limited in size by a configuration value (typically 1 gigabyte), so if a relation exceeds that size, it is split into multiple

segments.

For more information, see Section 73.1.

(Don't confuse this term with the similar term *[WAL segment](#page-196-3)*).

<span id="page-188-5"></span>Foreign data wrapper A means of representing data that is not contained in the local

*[database](#page-187-5)* so that it appears as if were in local *[table\(s\)](#page-194-0)*. With a foreign data wrapper it is possible to define a *[foreign server](#page-188-3)* and

*[foreign tables](#page-188-4)*.

For more information, see CREATE FOREIGN DATA WRAP-

PER.

<span id="page-188-9"></span>Foreign key A type of *[constraint](#page-186-2)* defined on one or more *[columns](#page-186-7)* in a *[table](#page-194-0)*

which requires the value(s) in those *[columns](#page-186-7)* to identify zero or

one *[row](#page-195-0)* in another (or, infrequently, the same) *[table](#page-194-0)*.

<span id="page-188-3"></span>Foreign server A named collection of *[foreign tables](#page-188-4)* which all use the same *[for-](#page-188-5)*

*[eign data wrapper](#page-188-5)* and have other configuration values in com-

mon.

For more information, see CREATE SERVER.

<span id="page-188-4"></span>Foreign table (relation) A *[relation](#page-191-0)* which appears to have *[rows](#page-195-0)* and *[columns](#page-186-7)* similar to a

regular *[table](#page-194-0)*, but will forward requests for data through its *[foreign](#page-188-5) [data wrapper](#page-188-5)*, which will return *[result sets](#page-192-2)* structured according

to the definition of the *[foreign table](#page-188-4)*.

For more information, see CREATE FOREIGN TABLE.

<span id="page-188-8"></span>Fork Each of the separate segmented file sets in which a relation is

stored. The *main fork* is where the actual data resides. There also exist two secondary forks for metadata: the *[free space map](#page-188-6)* and

the *[visibility map](#page-196-4)*. *[Unlogged relations](#page-195-3)* also have an *init fork*.

<span id="page-188-6"></span>Free space map (fork) A storage structure that keeps metadata about each data page of a

table's main fork. The free space map entry for each page stores the amount of free space that's available for future tuples, and is structured to be efficiently searched for available space for a new

tuple of a given size.

For more information, see Section 73.3.

<span id="page-188-1"></span>Function (routine) A type of routine that receives zero or more arguments, returns

zero or more output values, and is constrained to run within one transaction. Functions are invoked as part of a query, for example

2951

via SELECT. Certain functions can return *[sets](#page-192-2)*; those are called *set-returning functions*.

Functions can also be used for *[triggers](#page-195-4)* to invoke.

For more information, see CREATE FUNCTION.

GMT See [UTC.](#page-196-5)

Grant An SQL command that is used to allow a *[user](#page-195-1)* or *[role](#page-192-3)* to access

specific objects within the *[database](#page-187-5)*.

For more information, see GRANT.

Heap Contains the values of *[row](#page-195-0)* attributes (i.e., the data) for a *[relation](#page-191-0)*.

The heap is realized within one or more *[file segments](#page-188-7)* in the rela-

tion's *[main fork](#page-188-8)*.

Host A computer that communicates with other computers over a net-

work. This is sometimes used as a synonym for *[server](#page-193-3)*. It is also

used to refer to a computer where *[client processes](#page-186-8)* run.

<span id="page-189-3"></span>Index (relation) A *[relation](#page-191-0)* that contains data derived from a *[table](#page-194-0)* or *[materialized](#page-190-4)*

*[view](#page-190-4)*. Its internal structure supports fast retrieval of and access to

the original data.

For more information, see CREATE INDEX.

Insert An SQL command used to add new data into a *[table](#page-194-0)*.

For more information, see INSERT.

<span id="page-189-1"></span>Instance A group of *[backend](#page-184-5)* and *[auxiliary processes](#page-184-2)* that communicate

using a common shared memory area. One *[postmaster process](#page-191-3)* manages the instance; one instance manages exactly one *[database](#page-187-3) [cluster](#page-187-3)* with all its databases. Many instances can run on the same

*[server](#page-193-3)* as long as their TCP ports do not conflict.

The instance handles all key features of a DBMS: read and write access to files and shared memory, assurance of the ACID properties, *[connections](#page-186-4)* to *[client processes](#page-186-8)*, privilege verification, crash

recovery, replication, etc.

<span id="page-189-0"></span>Isolation The property that the effects of a transaction are not visible to *[con-](#page-186-9)*

*[current transactions](#page-186-9)* before it commits. This is one of the ACID

properties.

For more information, see Section 13.2.

Join An operation and SQL keyword used in *[queries](#page-191-2)* for combining

data from multiple *[relations](#page-191-0)*.

Key A means of identifying a *[row](#page-195-0)* within a *[table](#page-194-0)* or other *[relation](#page-191-0)* by

values contained within one or more *[attributes](#page-184-4)* in that relation.

Lock A mechanism that allows a process to limit or prevent simultane-

ous access to a resource.

<span id="page-189-2"></span>Log file Log files contain human-readable text lines about events. Exam-

ples include login failures, long-running queries, etc.

For more information, see Section 25.3.

<span id="page-190-5"></span>Logged A *[table](#page-194-0)* is considered *[logged](#page-190-5)* if changes to it are sent to the *[WAL](#page-197-4)*.

By default, all regular tables are logged. A table can be specified as *[unlogged](#page-195-3)* either at creation time or via the ALTER TABLE

command.

<span id="page-190-1"></span>Logger (process) An *[auxiliary process](#page-184-2)* which, if enabled, writes information about

database events into the current *[log file](#page-189-2)*. When reaching certain time- or volume-dependent criteria, a new log file is created. Also

called *syslogger*.

For more information, see Section 20.8.

Log record Archaic term for a *[WAL record](#page-196-6)*.

<span id="page-190-0"></span>Log sequence number (LSN) Byte offset into the *[WAL](#page-197-4)*, increasing monotonically with each new

*[WAL record](#page-196-6)*.

For more information, see pg\_lsn and Section 30.6.

LSN See [Log sequence number](#page-190-0).

Master (server) See [Primary \(server\).](#page-191-4)

Materialized The property that some information has been pre-computed and

stored for later use, rather than computing it on-the-fly.

This term is used in *[materialized view](#page-190-4)*, to mean that the data derived from the view's query is stored on disk separately from the

sources of that data.

This term is also used to refer to some multi-step queries to mean that the data resulting from executing a given step is stored in memory (with the possibility of spilling to disk), so that it can be

read multiple times by another step.

<span id="page-190-4"></span>Materialized view (relation) A *[relation](#page-191-0)* that is defined by a SELECT statement (just like a

*[view](#page-196-2)*), but stores data in the same way that a *[table](#page-194-0)* does. It cannot be modified via INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE opera-

tions.

For more information, see CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW.

Merge An SQL command used to conditionally add, modify, or remove

*[rows](#page-195-0)* in a given *[table](#page-194-0)*, using data from a source *[relation](#page-191-0)*.

For more information, see MERGE.

<span id="page-190-3"></span>Multi-version concurrency con-

trol (MVCC)

A mechanism designed to allow several *[transactions](#page-194-1)* to be reading and writing the same rows without one process causing other

processes to stall. In PostgreSQL, MVCC is implemented by creating copies (*versions*) of *[tuples](#page-195-0)* as they are modified; after transactions that can see the old versions terminate, those old versions

need to be removed.

<span id="page-190-6"></span>Null A concept of non-existence that is a central tenet of relational

database theory. It represents the absence of a definite value.

Optimizer See [Query planner](#page-191-1).

<span id="page-190-2"></span>Parallel query The ability to handle parts of executing a *[query](#page-191-2)* to take advantage

of parallel processes on servers with multiple CPUs.

<span id="page-191-6"></span>

Partition One of several disjoint (not overlapping) subsets of a larger set.

In reference to a *[partitioned table](#page-191-5)*: One of the tables that each contain part of the data of the partitioned table, which is said to be the *parent*. The partition is itself a table, so it can also be queried directly; at the same time, a partition can sometimes be a partitioned table, allowing hierarchies to be created.

In reference to a *[window function](#page-197-0)* in a *[query](#page-191-2)*, a partition is a userdefined criterion that identifies which neighboring *[rows](#page-195-0)* of the *[query's result set](#page-192-2)* can be considered by the function.

<span id="page-191-5"></span>

Partitioned table (relation) A *[relation](#page-191-0)* that is in semantic terms the same as a *[table](#page-194-0)*, but whose storage is distributed across several *[partitions](#page-191-6)*.

<span id="page-191-3"></span>

Postmaster (process) The very first process of an *[instance](#page-189-1)*. It starts and manages the *[auxiliary processes](#page-184-2)* and creates *[backend processes](#page-184-5)* on demand.

For more information, see Section 19.3.

<span id="page-191-7"></span>

Primary key A special case of a *[unique constraint](#page-195-5)* defined on a *[table](#page-194-0)* or other *[relation](#page-191-0)* that also guarantees that all of the *[attributes](#page-184-4)* within the *[primary key](#page-191-7)* do not have *[null](#page-190-6)* values. As the name implies, there can be only one primary key per table, though it is possible to have multiple unique constraints that also have no null-capable attributes.

<span id="page-191-4"></span>

Primary (server) When two or more *[databases](#page-187-5)* are linked via *[replication](#page-192-0)*, the *[server](#page-193-3)* that is considered the authoritative source of information is called the *primary*, also known as a *master*.

<span id="page-191-8"></span>

Procedure (routine) A type of routine. Their distinctive qualities are that they do not return values, and that they are allowed to make transactional statements such as COMMIT and ROLLBACK. They are invoked via the CALL command.

For more information, see CREATE PROCEDURE.

<span id="page-191-2"></span>

Query A request sent by a client to a *[backend](#page-184-5)*, usually to return results or to modify data on the database.

<span id="page-191-1"></span>

Query planner The part of PostgreSQL that is devoted to determining (*planning*) the most efficient way to execute *[queries](#page-191-2)*. Also known as *query optimizer*, *optimizer*, or simply *planner*.

Record See [Tuple](#page-195-0).

Recycling See [WAL file.](#page-196-3)

Referential integrity A means of restricting data in one *[relation](#page-191-0)* by a *[foreign key](#page-188-9)* so that it must have matching data in another *[relation](#page-191-0)*.

<span id="page-191-0"></span>

Relation The generic term for all objects in a *[database](#page-187-5)* that have a name and a list of *[attributes](#page-184-4)* defined in a specific order. *[Tables](#page-194-0)*, *[sequences](#page-193-4)*, *[views](#page-196-2)*, *[foreign tables](#page-188-4)*, *[materialized views](#page-190-4)*, composite types, and

*[indexes](#page-189-3)* are all relations.

More generically, a relation is a set of tuples; for example, the result of a query is also a relation.

In PostgreSQL, *Class* is an archaic synonym for *relation*.

<span id="page-192-4"></span>Replica (server) A *[database](#page-187-5)* that is paired with a *[primary](#page-191-4)* database and is main-

taining a copy of some or all of the primary database's data. The foremost reasons for doing this are to allow for greater access to that data, and to maintain availability of the data in the event that

the *[primary](#page-191-4)* becomes unavailable.

<span id="page-192-0"></span>Replication The act of reproducing data on one *[server](#page-193-3)* onto another server

called a *[replica](#page-192-4)*. This can take the form of *physical replication*, where all file changes from one server are copied verbatim, or *logical replication* where a defined subset of data changes are con-

veyed using a higher-level representation.

Restartpoint A variant of a *[checkpoint](#page-186-3)* performed on a *[replica](#page-192-4)*.

For more information, see Section 30.5.

<span id="page-192-2"></span>Result set A *[relation](#page-191-0)* transmitted from a *[backend process](#page-184-5)* to a *[client](#page-186-8)* upon the

completion of an SQL command, usually a SELECT but it can be an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE command if the RETURNING

clause is specified.

The fact that a result set is a relation means that a query can be used in the definition of another query, becoming a *subquery*.

Revoke A command to prevent access to a named set of *[database](#page-187-5)* objects

for a named list of *[roles](#page-192-3)*.

For more information, see REVOKE.

<span id="page-192-3"></span>Role A collection of access privileges to the *[instance](#page-187-5)*. Roles are them-

selves a privilege that can be granted to other roles. This is often done for convenience or to ensure completeness when multiple

*[users](#page-195-1)* need the same privileges.

For more information, see CREATE ROLE.

<span id="page-192-1"></span>Rollback A command to undo all of the operations performed since the be-

ginning of a *[transaction](#page-194-1)*.

For more information, see ROLLBACK.

Routine A defined set of instructions stored in the database system that

can be invoked for execution. A routine can be written in a variety of programming languages. Routines can be *[functions](#page-188-1)* (including set-returning functions and *[trigger functions](#page-195-4)*), *[aggregate](#page-184-6)*

*[functions](#page-184-6)*, and *[procedures](#page-191-8)*.

Many routines are already defined within PostgreSQL itself, but

user-defined ones can also be added.

Row See [Tuple](#page-195-0).

Savepoint A special mark in the sequence of steps in a *[transaction](#page-194-1)*. Data

modifications after this point in time may be reverted to the time

of the savepoint.

For more information, see SAVEPOINT.

<span id="page-192-5"></span>Schema A schema is a namespace for *[SQL objects](#page-193-2)*, which all reside in

the same *[database](#page-187-5)*. Each SQL object must reside in exactly one

schema.

All system-defined SQL objects reside in schema pg\_catalog.

More generically, the term *schema* is used to mean all data descriptions (*[table](#page-194-0)* definitions, *[constraints](#page-186-2)*, comments, etc.) for a given *[database](#page-187-5)* or subset thereof.

For more information, see Section 5.9.

Segment See [File segment](#page-188-7).

Select The SQL command used to request data from a *[database](#page-187-5)*. Normally, SELECT commands are not expected to modify the *[data](#page-187-5)[base](#page-187-5)* in any way, but it is possible that *[functions](#page-188-1)* invoked within the query could have side effects that do modify data.

For more information, see SELECT.

<span id="page-193-4"></span>

Sequence (relation) A type of relation that is used to generate values. Typically the generated values are sequential non-repeating numbers. They are commonly used to generate surrogate *[primary key](#page-191-7)* values.

<span id="page-193-3"></span>

Server A computer on which PostgreSQL *[instances](#page-189-1)* run. The term *server* denotes real hardware, a container, or a *virtual machine*.

This term is sometimes used to refer to an instance or to a host.

<span id="page-193-0"></span>

Session A state that allows a client and a backend to interact, communicating over a *[connection](#page-186-4)*.

<span id="page-193-1"></span>

Shared memory RAM which is used by the processes common to an *[instance](#page-189-1)*. It mirrors parts of *[database](#page-187-5)* files, provides a transient area for *[WAL records](#page-196-6)*, and stores additional common information. Note that shared memory belongs to the complete instance, not to a single database.

> The largest part of shared memory is known as *shared buffers* and is used to mirror part of data files, organized into pages. When a page is modified, it is called a dirty page until it is written back to the file system.

For more information, see Section 20.4.1.

<span id="page-193-2"></span>

SQL object Any object that can be created with a CREATE command. Most objects are specific to one database, and are commonly known as *local objects*.

> Most local objects reside in a specific *[schema](#page-192-5)* in their containing database, such as *[relations](#page-191-0)* (all types), *[routines](#page-188-1)* (all types), data types, etc. The names of such objects of the same type in the same schema are enforced to be unique.

> There also exist local objects that do not reside in schemas; some examples are *[extensions](#page-188-2)*, *[data type casts](#page-185-3)*, and *[foreign data wrap](#page-188-5)[pers](#page-188-5)*. The names of such objects of the same type are enforced to be unique within the database.

> Other object types, such as *[roles](#page-192-3)*, *[tablespaces](#page-194-4)*, replication origins, subscriptions for logical replication, and databases themselves are not local SQL objects since they exist entirely outside of any specific database; they are called *global objects*. The names of such

objects are enforced to be unique within the whole database cluster.

For more information, see Section 23.1.

<span id="page-194-5"></span>SQL standard A series of documents that define the SQL language.

Standby (server) See [Replica \(server\)](#page-192-4).

<span id="page-194-2"></span>Startup process An *[auxiliary process](#page-184-2)* that replays WAL during crash recovery and

in a *[physical replica](#page-192-0)*.

(The name is historical: the startup process was named before replication was implemented; the name refers to its task as it re-

lates to the server startup following a crash.)

Superuser As used in this documentation, it is a synonym for *[database su-](#page-187-4)*

*[peruser](#page-187-4)*.

<span id="page-194-3"></span>System catalog A collection of *[tables](#page-194-0)* which describe the structure of all *[SQL ob-](#page-193-2)*

*[jects](#page-193-2)* of the instance. The system catalog resides in the schema pg\_catalog. These tables contain data in internal representation and are not typically considered useful for user examination; a number of user-friendlier *[views](#page-196-2)*, also in schema pg\_catalog, offer more convenient access to some of that information, while additional tables and views exist in schema information\_schema (see Chapter 37) that expose some of the same and additional information as mandated by the *[SQL standard](#page-194-5)*.

For more information, see Section 5.9.

<span id="page-194-0"></span>Table A collection of *[tuples](#page-195-0)* having a common data structure (the same

number of *[attributes](#page-184-4)*, in the same order, having the same name and type per position). A table is the most common form of *[relation](#page-191-0)*

in PostgreSQL.

For more information, see CREATE TABLE.

<span id="page-194-4"></span>Tablespace A named location on the server file system. All *[SQL objects](#page-193-2)* which

require storage beyond their definition in the *[system catalog](#page-194-3)* must belong to a single tablespace. Initially, a database cluster contains a single usable tablespace which is used as the default for all SQL

objects, called pg\_default.

For more information, see Section 23.6.

<span id="page-194-6"></span>Temporary table *[Tables](#page-194-0)* that exist either for the lifetime of a *[session](#page-193-0)* or a *[transac-](#page-194-1)*

*[tion](#page-194-1)*, as specified at the time of creation. The data in them is not visible to other sessions, and is not *[logged](#page-190-5)*. Temporary tables are often used to store intermediate data for a multi-step operation.

For more information, see CREATE TABLE.

TOAST A mechanism by which large attributes of table rows are split and

stored in a secondary table, called the *TOAST table*. Each relation

with large attributes has its own TOAST table.

For more information, see Section 73.2.

<span id="page-194-1"></span>Transaction A combination of commands that must act as a single *[atomic](#page-184-7)* com-

mand: they all succeed or all fail as a single unit, and their effects

are not visible to other *[sessions](#page-193-0)* until the transaction is complete, and possibly even later, depending on the isolation level.

For more information, see Section 13.2.

<span id="page-195-2"></span>

Transaction ID The numerical, unique, sequentially-assigned identifier that each transaction receives when it first causes a database modification. Frequently abbreviated as *xid*. When stored on disk, xids are only 32-bits wide, so only approximately four billion write transaction IDs can be generated; to permit the system to run for longer than that, *epochs* are used, also 32 bits wide. When the counter reaches the maximum xid value, it starts over at 3 (values under that are reserved) and the epoch value is incremented by one. In some contexts, the epoch and xid values are considered together as a single 64-bit value; see Section 74.1 for more details.

For more information, see Section 8.19.

Transactions per second (TPS) Average number of transactions that are executed per second, totaled across all sessions active for a measured run. This is used as a measure of the performance characteristics of an instance.

<span id="page-195-4"></span>

Trigger A *[function](#page-188-1)* which can be defined to execute whenever a certain operation (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE) is applied to a *[relation](#page-191-0)*. A trigger executes within the same *[transaction](#page-194-1)* as the statement which invoked it, and if the function fails, then the invoking statement also fails.

For more information, see CREATE TRIGGER.

<span id="page-195-0"></span>

Tuple A collection of *[attributes](#page-184-4)* in a fixed order. That order may be defined by the *[table](#page-194-0)* (or other *[relation](#page-191-0)*) where the tuple is contained, in which case the tuple is often called a *row*. It may also be defined by the structure of a result set, in which case it is sometimes called a *record*.

<span id="page-195-5"></span>

Unique constraint A type of *[constraint](#page-186-2)* defined on a *[relation](#page-191-0)* which restricts the values allowed in one or a combination of columns so that each value or combination of values can only appear once in the relation that is, no other row in the relation contains values that are equal to those.

> Because *[null values](#page-190-6)* are not considered equal to each other, multiple rows with null values are allowed to exist without violating the unique constraint.

<span id="page-195-3"></span>

Unlogged The property of certain *[relations](#page-191-0)* that the changes to them are not reflected in the *[WAL](#page-197-4)*. This disables replication and crash recovery for these relations.

> The primary use of unlogged tables is for storing transient work data that must be shared across processes.

*[Temporary tables](#page-194-6)* are always unlogged.

Update An SQL command used to modify *[rows](#page-195-0)* that may already exist in a specified *[table](#page-194-0)*. It cannot create or remove rows.

For more information, see UPDATE.

<span id="page-195-1"></span>

User A *[role](#page-192-3)* that has the *login privilege* (see Section 22.2).

User mapping The translation of login credentials in the local *[database](#page-187-5)* to credentials in a remote data system defined by a *[foreign data wrap](#page-188-5)[per](#page-188-5)*.

For more information, see CREATE USER MAPPING.

<span id="page-196-5"></span>

UTC Universal Coordinated Time, the primary global time reference, approximately the time prevailing at the zero meridian of longitude. Often but inaccurately referred to as GMT (Greenwich Mean Time).

<span id="page-196-0"></span>

Vacuum The process of removing outdated *[tuple versions](#page-195-0)* from tables or materialized views, and other closely related processing required by PostgreSQL's implementation of *[MVCC](#page-190-3)*. This can be initiated through the use of the VACUUM command, but can also be handled automatically via *[autovacuum](#page-184-3)* processes.

For more information, see Section 25.1 .

<span id="page-196-2"></span>View A *[relation](#page-191-0)* that is defined by a SELECT statement, but has no storage of its own. Any time a query references a view, the definition of the view is substituted into the query as if the user had typed it as a subquery instead of the name of the view.

For more information, see CREATE VIEW.

<span id="page-196-4"></span>

Visibility map (fork) A storage structure that keeps metadata about each data page of a table's main fork. The visibility map entry for each page stores two bits: the first one (all-visible) indicates that all tuples in the page are visible to all transactions. The second one (allfrozen) indicates that all tuples in the page are marked frozen.

WAL See [Write-ahead log.](#page-197-4)

<span id="page-196-1"></span>

WAL archiver (process) An *[auxiliary process](#page-184-2)* which, if enabled, saves copies of *[WAL files](#page-196-3)* for the purpose of creating backups or keeping *[replicas](#page-192-4)* current.

For more information, see Section 26.3.

<span id="page-196-3"></span>

WAL file Also known as *WAL segment* or *WAL segment file*. Each of the sequentially-numbered files that provide storage space for *[WAL](#page-197-4)*. The files are all of the same predefined size and are written in sequential order, interspersing changes as they occur in multiple simultaneous sessions. If the system crashes, the files are read in order, and each of the changes is replayed to restore the system to the state it was in before the crash.

> Each WAL file can be released after a *[checkpoint](#page-186-3)* writes all the changes in it to the corresponding data files. Releasing the file can be done either by deleting it, or by changing its name so that it will be used in the future, which is called *recycling*.

For more information, see Section 30.6.

<span id="page-196-6"></span>

WAL record A low-level description of an individual data change. It contains sufficient information for the data change to be re-executed (*replayed*) in case a system failure causes the change to be lost. WAL records use a non-printable binary format.

For more information, see Section 30.6.

<span id="page-197-1"></span>WAL receiver (process) An *[auxiliary process](#page-184-2)* that runs on a *[replica](#page-192-4)* to receive WAL from

the *[primary server](#page-191-4)* for replay by the *[startup process](#page-194-2)*.

For more information, see Section 27.2.

WAL segment See [WAL file.](#page-196-3)

<span id="page-197-2"></span>WAL sender (process) A special *[backend process](#page-184-5)* that streams WAL over a network. The

receiving end can be a *[WAL receiver](#page-197-1)* in a *[replica](#page-192-4)*, pg\_receivewal, or any other client program that speaks the replication protocol.

<span id="page-197-3"></span>WAL writer (process) An *[auxiliary process](#page-184-2)* that writes *[WAL records](#page-196-6)* from *[shared mem-](#page-193-1)*

*[ory](#page-193-1)* to *[WAL files](#page-196-3)*.

For more information, see Section 20.5.

<span id="page-197-0"></span>Window function (routine) A type of *[function](#page-188-1)* used in a *[query](#page-191-2)* that applies to a *[partition](#page-191-6)* of the

query's *[result set](#page-192-2)*; the function's result is based on values found in

*[rows](#page-195-0)* of the same partition or frame.

All *[aggregate functions](#page-184-6)* can be used as window functions, but window functions can also be used to, for example, give ranks to each of the rows in the partition. Also known as *analytic functions*.

For more information, see Section 3.5.

<span id="page-197-4"></span>Write-ahead log The journal that keeps track of the changes in the *[database cluster](#page-187-3)*

as user- and system-invoked operations take place. It comprises many individual *[WAL records](#page-196-6)* written sequentially to *[WAL files](#page-196-3)*.

# **Appendix N. Color Support**

Most programs in the PostgreSQL package can produce colorized console output. This appendix describes how that is configured.

# **N.1. When Color is Used**

To use colorized output, set the environment variable PG\_COLOR as follows:

- 1. If the value is always, then color is used.
- 2. If the value is auto and the standard error stream is associated with a terminal device, then color is used.
- 3. Otherwise, color is not used.

# **N.2. Configuring the Colors**

The actual colors to be used are configured using the environment variable PG\_COLORS (note plural). The value is a colon-separated list of key=value pairs. The keys specify what the color is to be used for. The values are SGR (Select Graphic Rendition) specifications, which are interpreted by the terminal.

The following keys are currently in use:

error

used to highlight the text "error" in error messages

warning

used to highlight the text "warning" in warning messages

note

used to highlight the text "detail" and "hint" in such messages

locus

used to highlight location information (e.g., program name and file name) in messages

The default value is error=01;31:warning=01;35:note=01;36:locus=01 (01;31 = bold red, 01;35 = bold magenta, 01;36 = bold cyan, 01 = bold default color).

### **Tip**

This color specification format is also used by other software packages such as GCC, GNU coreutils, and GNU grep.

# **Appendix O. Obsolete or Renamed Features**

Functionality is sometimes removed from PostgreSQL, feature, setting and file names sometimes change, or documentation moves to different places. This section directs users coming from old versions of the documentation or from external links to the appropriate new location for the information they need.

# **O.1. recovery.conf file merged into postgresql.conf**

PostgreSQL 11 and below used a configuration file named recovery.conf to manage replicas and standbys. Support for this file was removed in PostgreSQL 12. See the release notes for PostgreSQL 12 for details on this change.

On PostgreSQL 12 and above, archive recovery, streaming replication, and PITR are configured using normal server configuration parameters. These are set in postgresql.conf or via ALTER SYSTEM like any other parameter.

The server will not start if a recovery.conf exists.

PostgreSQL 15 and below had a setting promote\_trigger\_file, or trigger\_file before 12. Use pg\_ctl promote or call pg\_promote() to promote a standby instead.

The standby\_mode setting has been removed. A standby.signal file in the data directory is used instead. See Standby Server Operation for details.

# **O.2. Default Roles Renamed to Predefined Roles**

PostgreSQL 13 and below used the term "Default Roles". However, as these roles are not able to actually be changed and are installed as part of the system at initialization time, the more appropriate term to use is "Predefined Roles". See Section 22.5 for current documentation regarding Predefined Roles, and the release notes for PostgreSQL 14 for details on this change.

# **O.3. pg\_xlogdump renamed to pg\_waldump**

PostgreSQL 9.6 and below provided a command named pg\_xlogdump to read write-ahead-log (WAL) files. This command was renamed to pg\_waldump, see pg\_waldump for documentation of pg\_waldump and see the release notes for PostgreSQL 10 for details on this change.

# **O.4. pg\_resetxlog renamed to pg\_resetwal**

PostgreSQL 9.6 and below provided a command named pg\_resetxlog to reset the write-aheadlog (WAL) files. This command was renamed to pg\_resetwal, see pg\_resetwal for documentation of pg\_resetwal and see the release notes for PostgreSQL 10 for details on this change.

# **O.5. pg\_receivexlog renamed to pg\_receivewal**
